section: bandits and exploration in one screen
text: Bandits and exploration in one screen An agent that learns from its own actions has to keep choosing between exploiting the action it currently believes is best and exploring an action that might be better.
label: core

section: bandits and exploration in one screen
text: The cleanest form of the problem is the multi-armed bandit : one state, k actions with unknown average payoffs, and a score for the total reward collected.
label: core

section: bandits and exploration in one screen
text: Bandits have a precise yardstick, regret , and a proven floor on it: any good strategy must lose reward growing at least like the logarithm of time.
label: core

section: bandits and exploration in one screen
text: The strategies below differ in how they spend that loss.
label: fat

text: 1 The exploration-exploitation trade-off Exploitation uses current knowledge to take the action believed best, maximising reward now.
label: core

text: Exploration takes an action that looks worse, to gather information that may pay off later.
label: core
key: buy information that may pay later

text: Silver's everyday examples ( Silver, Lecture 9 ): go to your favourite restaurant or try a new one; show the most successful advert or a different one; drill for oil at the best known site or at a new one; play the move you believe is best or an experimental one.
label: core

text: Pure exploitation gets stuck on the first decent option it finds, because it never collects the evidence that something else is better.
label: core
key: stuck on the first decent option

text: Pure exploration never cashes in what it has learned.
label: core

text: Why this is special to reinforcement learning: in supervised learning the training labels arrive whatever the model predicts.
label: core
key: the labels arrive whatever the model predicts

text: Here the agent's own choices decide which data it sees , so a wrong belief about an action can never be corrected if the agent stops taking it.
label: core
key: the agent's own choices decide which data it sees

text: The value of trying an action is therefore partly the reward it pays now and partly the information it buys.
label: fat

text: Bandits isolate this: one situation repeated, no state, no delay between action and reward, so nothing is left except exploration ( Sutton and Barto, chapter 2 ).
label: core

text: There is a sense in which the trade-off is "solved": if you have a prior over the arms and a known horizon, the best possible policy is the Bayes-optimal one, computed by planning over all future beliefs.
label: depth

text: It is almost never computed, because the tree of possible futures explodes; Sutton and Barto note that for 1,000 steps of a two-armed bandit with two possible rewards the tree would have 2 2000 leaves ( §2.10 ).
label: depth

text: For the discounted, infinite-horizon case, Gittins (1979) showed that the Bayes-optimal policy reduces to an index computed per arm.
label: depth

text: Everything else on this page is a cheaper rule that gets close.
label: depth
key: a cheaper rule that gets close

text: 2 The k-armed bandit and action values At each step t the agent picks an action A t from k options and receives a reward R t drawn from that action's distribution.
label: core

section: 2 the k-armed bandit and action values
text: The value of an action is its expected reward, q *( a ) = E[ R t | A t = a ]; if the agent knew it, the problem would be trivial.

text: 3 The strategies Greedy and ε-greedy Greedy always takes argmax a Q t ( a ) (ties broken at random).
label: core

text: It locks onto whichever arm looked good first. ε-greedy takes the greedy action with probability 1 − ε and otherwise picks uniformly among all m actions, so the greedy action has probability 1 − ε + ε/ m and each other action ε/ m ; with ε = 0.1 and m = 4 that is 0.9 + 0.025 = 0.925 and 0.025 ( Silver, Lecture 5 ).
label: core

text: Every action is tried infinitely often, so every estimate converges; the price is that ε-greedy keeps picking bad arms at the same rate forever, so its regret grows linearly.
label: core

text: Decaying ε towards 0 while still trying every action infinitely often is called GLIE (greedy in the limit with infinite exploration); it is the condition under which Monte Carlo control and SARSA converge to the optimal policy ( Silver, Lecture 5 ; Model-free prediction and control ).
label: core

text: Optimistic initial values Set every initial estimate far above any plausible reward (Sutton and Barto use +5 when the true values are drawn from N(0, 1)).
label: core

text: Whatever the greedy agent tries disappoints it, so it moves on to the next arm, and every arm is tried several times before the estimates settle ( §2.6 ).
label: core
key: every arm is tried several times

text: It needs a constant step size: with sample averages the optimism is erased by the first pull of each arm.
label: core
key: erases the optimism on the first pull

text: The book calls it "a simple trick that can be quite effective on stationary problems, but it is far from being a generally useful approach": its drive to explore is spent at the start, so it cannot respond when the task changes.
label: core
key: far from being a generally useful approach

text: The same idea, made principled, is R-MAX in full RL (section 6).
label: core

text: Upper confidence bound (UCB) ε-greedy explores indiscriminately.
label: core

text: Better: prefer arms that could plausibly be the best, given how uncertain their estimates are ( §2.7, eq.
label: core

text: Thompson sampling Keep a posterior distribution over each arm's mean.
label: core

text: At every step draw one sample from each posterior and pull the arm whose sample is highest; update that arm's posterior with the reward.
label: core
key: pull the arm whose sample is highest

text: An arm is pulled with exactly the probability that it is the best arm under the current belief ("probability matching").
label: core

text: For 0/1 rewards with a uniform prior the posterior is Beta(1 + successes, 1 + failures), so the whole algorithm is two counters per arm and one Beta draw.
label: core

text: It is the oldest method on the page: Thompson (1933) proposed it "for allocating experimental effort in two-armed bandit problems arising in clinical trials" ( Russo et al., tutorial ).
label: core

text: Uncertain arms have wide posteriors, so they sometimes produce a high draw and get tried; as evidence accumulates a bad arm's posterior narrows below the best arm's and it stops being chosen.
label: core

text: Sutton and Barto note that it "often performs similarly to the best of the distribution-free methods" ( §2.10 ).
label: core
key: often performs similarly to the best of the distribution-free methods

section: 4 regret, and the floor under it
text: The theory asks a sharper question: on any task, how much reward does a strategy lose against an oracle that always pulls the best arm?
label: core
key: an oracle that always pulls the best arm

section: 4 regret, and the floor under it
text: That loss is the regret : Regret(T) = T μ* − E[ Σ t=1..T μ A t ] = Σ a Δ a E[N a (T)] μ* the best arm's mean; Δ a = μ* − μ a is arm a's gap N a (T) how often arm a is pulled in T steps; the second form (the regret decomposition, Lattimore and Szepesvári, Lemma 4.5 ) says regret is just the pulls wasted on each bad arm times its gap A strategy that pulls a bad arm a fixed fraction of the time (greedy stuck on it, ε-greedy with fixed ε) has regret growing linearly in T.
label: core

section: 4 regret, and the floor under it
text: The question is how slowly it can grow.
label: fat

section: 4 regret, and the floor under it
text: The Lai and Robbins lower bound ( Lai and Robbins 1985 ): for any strategy that is good on every instance (its regret is o(T a ) for every a > 0), each suboptimal arm must be pulled at least about ln T / KL( p a , p *) times, so lim inf T→∞ Regret(T) / ln T ≥ Σ a: Δ a > 0 Δ a / KL(p a , p*) KL(p a , p*) the Kullback-Leibler divergence between arm a's reward distribution and the best arm's: how many bits each pull gives towards telling them apart.
label: core

section: 4 regret, and the floor under it
text: For 0/1 rewards KL(p, q) = p ln(p/q) + (1 − p) ln((1 − p)/(1 − q)) The intuition: to be sure an arm is worse, you must pull it until the evidence rules out that it is the best one, and the number of pulls that takes grows with how sure you need to be (ln T) and shrinks with how distinguishable the arms are (KL).
label: core

section: 4 regret, and the floor under it
text: Arms that are close (small Δ, small KL) are both cheap to confuse and expensive to separate.
label: fat

section: 4 regret, and the floor under it
text: The bound is asymptotic : it fixes the slope against ln T as T grows without limit, not the regret at any finite T.

text: 6 Exploration in full RL With states, an exploratory action's payoff may only show up many steps later, after a specific sequence of further actions.
label: core

text: That changes the problem in three ways.
label: fat

text: Dithering is exponentially slow. ε-greedy and softmax noise explore one step at a time.
label: core

text: If a reward sits at the end of a chain of N decisions where only one of two actions keeps you on track, a uniformly random policy reaches it with probability 2 −N per attempt, so it needs about 2 N attempts derived .
label: core

text: What is needed is deep (temporally extended) exploration: commit to a plan for finding out, across many steps.
label: core

text: Osband et al. put it this way: "Unlike dithering strategies such as epsilon-greedy exploration, bootstrapped DQN carries out temporally-extended (or deep) exploration; this can lead to exponentially faster learning" ( Osband et al.
label: core

text: Sparse rewards give no gradient.
label: core

text: If almost every episode returns 0, every action looks the same and value estimates have nothing to learn from until something succeeds by chance.
label: core
